spam-musubi.name: Spam musubi
spam-musubi.summary: A Hawaiian snack food of grilled Spam on rice wrapped in nori, in the style of Japanese onigiri, common in convenience stores and plate lunches.

loco-moco.name: Loco moco
loco-moco.summary: A Hawaiian dish of white rice topped with a hamburger patty, brown gravy and a fried egg, part of contemporary Hawaiian cuisine.

plate-lunch.name: Plate lunch
plate-lunch.summary: A Hawaiian meal blending Polynesian, North American and East Asian cuisine, typically rice, macaroni salad and an entrée such as chicken katsu or teriyaki.

pipikaula.name: Pipikaula
pipikaula.summary: A Hawaiian dish of salted, dried beef similar to jerky, traditionally eaten by Hawaii's paniolo cowboys.

leonard-s-bakery.name: Leonard's Bakery
leonard-s-bakery.summary: A Portuguese bakery in Honolulu, Hawaii, opened in 1952, credited with popularizing the malasada, a fried Hawaiian pastry brought by Portuguese immigrants around 1900; now known across the US and abroad.

malassada.name: Malassada
malassada.summary: Portuguese fried doughnut from Madeira, coated in sugar and cinnamon, brought to Hawaii by Portuguese plantation workers.

omiyage.name: Omiyage
omiyage.summary: The Japanese tradition of bringing back regional food gifts from a trip to share with family, friends and colleagues, often bought at transportation hubs.

faraoa-ipo.name: Faraoa 'ipo
faraoa-ipo.summary: A type of ball bread made in French Polynesia's Tuamotu archipelago from yeast-leavened flour with coconut, cooked in coconut water or an earth oven.

tuamotus.name: Tuamotu Islands
tuamotus.summary: French Polynesian chain of nearly 80 islands and atolls, the largest chain of atolls in the world, settled by Polynesians and home to about 16,000 people.

urapmin-people.name: Urapmin
urapmin-people.summary: A small ethnic group of about 375 people in Papua New Guinea who lived by hunting, gathering and taro farming, and once practiced cannibalism against enemies in war.

royal-hawaiian-hotel.name: Royal Hawaiian Hotel
royal-hawaiian-hotel.summary: A beachfront luxury hotel in Waikiki, Honolulu, one of the first hotels built there, nicknamed 'The Pink Palace of the Pacific' for its pink Spanish/Moorish-styled façade.

waik-k.name: Waikiki
waik-k.summary: A Honolulu neighborhood and largely man-made beach on Oahu's south shore, and the first capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii from 1795 to 1796.

hapa-haole-music.name: Hapa haole music
hapa-haole-music.summary: A Hawaiian music genre that grew to include swing, rock and rap, and became hugely popular on the US mainland in the 1910s as an image of Hawaii as an exotic vacation paradise.

tiki-culture.name: Tiki culture
tiki-culture.summary: An American art and entertainment movement begun in 1930s California, inspired by Polynesian and other Pacific cultures and seen in themed bars and decor.

warren-and-wetmore.name: Warren and Wetmore
warren-and-wetmore.summary: A New York architecture firm founded around 1889 by Whitney Warren and Charles D. Wetmore, with an extensive practice especially known for designing large hotels.

sonny-cunha.name: Sonny Cunha
sonny-cunha.summary: An American composer, bandleader and pianist (1879–1933) credited with popularizing hapa haole music, Hawaiian songs blending English and Hawaiian lyrics.

the-bird-of-paradise-play.name: The Bird of Paradise
the-bird-of-paradise-play.summary: A 1912 American play set in Hawaii, credited with spreading an image of Hawaii as a land of hula dancing, ukuleles, grass huts and volcano gods.

panama-pacific-international-exposition.name: Panama-Pacific International Exposition
panama-pacific-international-exposition.summary: A 1915 world's fair in San Francisco celebrating the completion of the Panama Canal and the city's recovery from the 1906 earthquake.

matson-inc.name: Matson
matson-inc.summary: An American ocean shipping company founded in 1882, running service from the U.S. to Hawaii, Alaska and other Pacific destinations.

castle-cooke.name: Castle & Cooke
castle-cooke.summary: A Los Angeles company once among Hawaii's 'Big Five,' historically active in agriculture and later merged into the Dole Food Company before shifting into real estate.

ss-malolo.name: SS Malolo
ss-malolo.summary: A luxury American passenger liner built in 1926 for the Matson Line, the largest of its era, that helped develop tourism to Hawaii.

waialae-country-club.name: Waialae Country Club
waialae-country-club.summary: A private golf club in East Honolulu founded in 1927, host of the PGA Tour's Sony Open in Hawaii since 1965 and originally built for guests of a luxury beach hotel.

harry-owens.name: Harry Owens
harry-owens.summary: American composer and bandleader (1902–1986) best known for writing the song "Sweet Leilani".

sweet-leilani.name: Sweet Leilani
sweet-leilani.summary: A 1937 song from the film Waikiki Wedding, written by Harry Owens for his newborn daughter, that won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.

bing-crosby.name: Bing Crosby
bing-crosby.summary: An American singer and actor (1903–1977) considered one of the most popular and influential musical artists of the 20th century, recording over 1,600 songs and appearing in more than 70 films.

waikiki-wedding.name: Waikiki Wedding
waikiki-wedding.summary: A 1937 American musical film starring Bing Crosby, remembered for the Academy Award-winning song 'Sweet Leilani' and for promoting tourism to the Territory of Hawaii.

moruroa.name: Moruroa
moruroa.summary: An atoll in French Polynesia's Tuamotu Archipelago where France conducted nuclear weapons tests between 1966 and 1996, sparking international protests.

fangataufa.name: Fangataufa
fangataufa.summary: An uninhabited coral atoll in French Polynesia used by France as a nuclear test site from 1966 to 1996, with 14 explosions carried out there.

sms-scharnhorst.name: SMS Scharnhorst
sms-scharnhorst.summary: The lead armored cruiser of the Imperial German Navy's East Asia Squadron, commissioned in 1907, which won the Battle of Coronel in 1914.

sms-gneisenau.name: SMS Gneisenau
sms-gneisenau.summary: An armored cruiser of the Imperial German Navy, launched in 1906, that served with the East Asia Squadron in the Pacific during World War I.

papeete.name: Papeete
papeete.summary: The capital of French Polynesia, on the island of Tahiti, and the territory's main center of government, commerce and tourism; its name means 'water from a basket.'

french-gunboat-z-l-e.name: Zélée
french-gunboat-z-l-e.summary: A French Navy gunboat used in Indochina and the Pacific, sunk while patrolling Tahiti during the German bombardment of Papeete on 22 September 1914.

wake-island.name: Wake Island
wake-island.summary: A coral atoll in the Pacific and unincorporated US territory, seized by Japan in a World War II battle in December 1941 and held until September 1945.

midway-atoll.name: Midway Atoll
midway-atoll.summary: A small atoll and U.S. territory in the North Pacific, site of a major World War II battle that helped turn the tide of the Pacific War.

united-states-minor-outlying-islands.name: United States Minor Outlying Islands
united-states-minor-outlying-islands.summary: A statistical designation for eight small U.S. Pacific islands, including Wake and Midway, plus Navassa Island in the Caribbean, several with major World War II history.

jacques-chirac.name: Jacques Chirac
jacques-chirac.summary: President of France from 1995 to 2007, previously Prime Minister and Mayor of Paris, known for opposing the American-led invasion of Iraq.

christopher-cradock.name: Christopher Cradock
christopher-cradock.summary: English Royal Navy rear-admiral (1862–1914) killed at the Battle of Coronel while hunting a German squadron in November 1914.

battle-of-coronel.name: Battle of Coronel
battle-of-coronel.summary: A First World War naval battle on 1 November 1914 off Chile in which a German squadron under Maximilian von Spee defeated a British force, a shock that led Britain to send ships that later destroyed the German fleet.

east-asia-squadron.name: German East Asia Squadron
east-asia-squadron.summary: An Imperial German Navy cruiser squadron active mainly in the Pacific from the mid-1890s until its destruction at the Battle of the Falkland Islands in 1914.

maximilian-von-spee.name: Maximilian von Spee
maximilian-von-spee.summary: German admiral who commanded the East Asia Squadron in World War I, defeating the British at the Battle of Coronel in 1914 before being killed, with two of his sons, at the Battle of the Falkland Islands.

battle-of-the-falkland-islands.name: Battle of the Falkland Islands
battle-of-the-falkland-islands.summary: A First World War naval battle on 8 December 1914 off the Falkland Islands, where a British squadron hunted down and destroyed most of the German cruiser squadron that had earlier won at Coronel.

johnston-atoll.name: Johnston Atoll
johnston-atoll.summary: Unincorporated US territory under Air Force jurisdiction, used since 1934 as a naval depot, airbase, and site for testing and disposing of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons.

nuku-hiva.name: Nuku Hiva
nuku-hiva.summary: The largest of the Marquesas Islands in French Polynesia, where Herman Melville set part of his book Typee.

robert-dean-frisbie.name: Robert Dean Frisbie
robert-dean-frisbie.summary: Robert Dean Frisbie: American writer of travel literature about Polynesia (1896-1948).

robert-louis-stevenson.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
robert-louis-stevenson.summary: Scottish novelist, poet and travel writer (1850-1894) known for Treasure Island, Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and Kidnapped; he settled in Samoa in 1890, where his writing turned darker.

pukapuka.name: Pukapuka
pukapuka.summary: A remote coral atoll in the northern Cook Islands, home to about 400 people who have preserved a distinct ancient culture and language over many centuries.

suwarrow.name: Suwarrow
suwarrow.summary: A remote island in the northern group of the Cook Islands in the South Pacific, about 810 miles south of the equator.

lori-matsukawa.name: Lori Matsukawa
lori-matsukawa.summary: An American television journalist who spent thirty-six years as evening news anchor at Seattle's KING 5, later writing a memoir, Being There: Memoir of an Asian American Journalist.

james-a-michener.name: James A. Michener
james-a-michener.summary: An American writer (1907-1997) of over 40 books, mostly long historical family sagas, who won the 1948 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for Tales of the South Pacific.

max-von-sydow.name: Max von Sydow
max-von-sydow.summary: Swedish and French actor (1929–2020) with a 70-year career, best known for roles in Ingmar Bergman's films and later Hollywood movies such as The Exorcist.

julie-andrews.name: Julie Andrews
julie-andrews.summary: English actress and singer, born 1935, known for starring in Mary Poppins and The Sound of Music and winning an Academy Award among many other honors.

charles-nordhoff.name: Charles Nordhoff
charles-nordhoff.summary: American novelist and traveler (1887–1947), born in England, best known for The Bounty Trilogy including Mutiny on the Bounty, co-written with James Norman Hall while both lived on Tahiti.

james-norman-hall.name: James Norman Hall
james-norman-hall.summary: American writer (1887–1951) who co-authored The Bounty Trilogy, including Mutiny on the Bounty, after settling in Tahiti following World War I service.

tom-neale.name: Tom Neale
tom-neale.summary: A New Zealander (1902-1977) who spent 16 years across three periods living alone on Anchorage Island in the Suwarrow atoll, Cook Islands, and wrote a popular autobiography about it.

johnny-frisbie.name: Johnny Frisbie
johnny-frisbie.summary: Cook Islands author (born 1932) whose autobiographical children's novel Miss Ulysses of Puka-Puka (1948) was the first published literary work by a Pacific Islander woman.

pukapukan-language.name: Pukapukan
pukapukan-language.summary: A Polynesian language that developed in isolation on Pukapuka atoll in the Cook Islands, closely linked to western Polynesian languages and now mostly spoken in migrant communities abroad.

american-samoa.name: American Samoa
american-samoa.summary: An unincorporated U.S. territory in the South Pacific made up of several Samoan islands, with a population of about 47,400, mostly indigenous Samoans.

avatiu.name: Avatiu
avatiu.summary: A settlement on the north coast of Rarotonga in the Cook Islands, home to the island's main harbour and fishing port.

the-forum-american-magazine.name: The Forum
the-forum-american-magazine.summary: American magazine founded in 1885, known for symposium-style debates on political and social issues from prominent guest authors, published in New York until 1950.

okina.name: ʻOkina
okina.summary: The letter used in written Hawaiian to represent the glottal stop sound, shown as a reversed apostrophe-like mark.

macron-diacritic.name: Kahakō
macron-diacritic.summary: A diacritical mark, a straight bar placed above a letter, originally used in Greco-Roman metrics to mark long syllables and now most often a long vowel.

partners-in-development-foundation.name: Partners In Development Foundation
partners-in-development-foundation.summary: A Hawaii-based nonprofit founded in 1997 that runs education and cultural programs, including Hawaiian-language preservation projects.

thor-heyerdahl.name: Thor Heyerdahl
thor-heyerdahl.summary: A Norwegian adventurer and ethnographer (1914–2002) famed for the 1947 Kon-Tiki raft voyage across the Pacific, aiming to show ancient trans-oceanic contact.

kon-tiki-expedition.name: Kon-Tiki expedition
kon-tiki-expedition.summary: A 1947 raft voyage across the Pacific from South America to Polynesia led by Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl, named after the Inca god Viracocha.

isabella-abbott.name: Isabella Abbott
isabella-abbott.summary: Hawaiian phycologist and ethnobotanist (1919–2010), the first Native Hawaiian woman to earn a science PhD, who became a leading expert on Pacific marine algae.

frank-der-yuen.name: Frank Der Yuen
frank-der-yuen.summary: American aeronautical engineer (1912–1984) who invented the jet bridge, also known as the passenger boarding bridge; graduated from MIT in 1933.

jet-bridge.name: Jet bridge
jet-bridge.summary: An enclosed, often extendable connector from an airport terminal gate to an airplane, letting passengers board and disembark without going outside; invented by Frank Der Yuen.

h-k-le-a.name: Hōkūleʻa
h-k-le-a.summary: Polynesian double-hulled voyaging canoe launched in 1975, famed for a 1976 voyage from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti using only traditional navigation, meant partly to help revive Polynesian culture.

polynesian-navigation.name: Wayfinding
polynesian-navigation.summary: Traditional Polynesian navigation techniques for long ocean voyages, using the stars, ocean swells, wind patterns and bird behavior, passed down through oral tradition rather than instruments.

natural-energy-laboratory-of-hawaii-auth.name: Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority
natural-energy-laboratory-of-hawaii-auth.summary: Hawaii state authority founded in 1974 that administers an industrial park researching uses of deep ocean water, including energy production and aquaculture, on the Big Island's Kona coast.
natural-energy-laboratory-of-hawaii-auth.source_title: Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority

mau-movement.name: Mau movement
mau-movement.summary: A non-violent movement for Samoan independence from colonial rule in the early-to-mid 20th century, whose 1929 protest 'Black Saturday' ended with New Zealand police killing Samoans.

overthrow-of-the-hawaiian-kingdom.name: Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom
overthrow-of-the-hawaiian-kingdom.summary: The January 1893 coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani that ended the Hawaiian Kingdom, leading to the Republic of Hawaii and eventual U.S. annexation in 1898; Congress formally apologized for it in 1993.

apology-resolution.name: Apology Resolution
apology-resolution.summary: A 1993 U.S. congressional resolution acknowledging America's role in overthrowing the Kingdom of Hawaii, later cited as impetus for the Hawaiian sovereignty movement.

bill-clinton.name: Bill Clinton
bill-clinton.summary: An American politician who served as the 42nd president of the United States from 1993 to 2001, after serving as governor of Arkansas in two non-consecutive periods, 1979 to 1981 and 1983 to 1992.

high-commissioner-for-the-western-pacifi.name: Western Pacific High Commission
high-commissioner-for-the-western-pacifi.summary: A British colonial office overseeing the western Pacific from 1877, based in Fiji until 1952 and then the Solomon Islands, later gaining supervisory power over British protectorates.
high-commissioner-for-the-western-pacifi.source_title: High Commissioner for the Western Pacific

bengt-danielsson.name: Bengt Danielsson
bengt-danielsson.summary: Swedish anthropologist and writer (1921–1997), crew member on the 1947 Kon-Tiki raft expedition, later awarded the Right Livelihood Award for opposing French nuclear tests.

right-livelihood-award.name: Right Livelihood Award
right-livelihood-award.summary: An international award established in 1980 by philanthropist Jakob von Uexküll, honouring practical answers to urgent challenges such as environmental protection and human rights, often called an 'Alternative Nobel Prize'.

seru-epenisa-cakobau.name: Seru Epenisa Cakobau
seru-epenisa-cakobau.summary: Fijian chief and warlord who united part of Fiji's warring tribes into a kingdom, serving as its only king from 1871 to 1874.

malietoa.name: Malietoa
malietoa.summary: One of Samoa's four paramount chiefly titles, meaning "great warrior," held by the head of one of Samoa's two great royal families.

malietoa-tanumafili-ii.name: Malietoa Tanumafili II
malietoa-tanumafili-ii.summary: Head of state of Samoa from its independence in 1962 until his death in 2007, having held the Malietoa title since 1940.

hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.name: Hawaiian sovereignty movement
hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.summary: A grassroots political and cultural campaign to reestablish an autonomous or independent Hawaiian nation, often seeking redress for the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom.

tafa-ifa.name: Tafaʻifa
tafa-ifa.summary: The highest title of the Samoan aristocracy, dominant in Samoan politics from the 16th century until it was disrupted by colonial intervention in the early 1900s.

mauna-kea.name: Mauna Kea
mauna-kea.summary: A dormant volcano on Hawaii's Big Island and the state's highest point, considered sacred in Native Hawaiian religion and the site of protests over telescope construction.

ho-oponopono.name: Hoʻoponopono
ho-oponopono.summary: A traditional Hawaiian practice of reconciliation and forgiveness, meaning 'correction'; similar forgiveness practices exist elsewhere in the South Pacific.

mary-kawena-pukui.name: Mary Kawena Pukui
mary-kawena-pukui.summary: Hawaiian scholar, author, composer, hula expert and educator (1895–1986), known as Kawena.

k-ne.name: Kāne
k-ne.summary: The highest of the three major Hawaiian deities, worshipped as the god of procreation, creator of life, and ancestor of chiefs and commoners, associated with dawn, sun and sky.

k.name: Kū
k.summary: One of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion, worshiped under many names including Kūkāʻilimoku, whose rites uniquely included human sacrifice.

lono.name: Lono
lono.summary: A Hawaiian god of fertility, agriculture, rain, music and peace, honored during the annual Makahiki festival.

kanaloa.name: Kanaloa
kanaloa.summary: A Hawaiian god symbolized by the squid or octopus, associated with the ocean and seamanship, and traditionally paired with the god Kāne.

american-indian-religious-freedom-act.name: American Indian Religious Freedom Act
american-indian-religious-freedom-act.summary: A 1978 U.S. law restoring religious liberties to American Indians, Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiians, protecting access to sacred sites and traditional ceremonies after such practices had long been banned.

thirty-meter-telescope.name: Thirty Meter Telescope
thirty-meter-telescope.summary: A proposed extremely large telescope for Mauna Kea in Hawaii, with a 492-segment mirror nine times more powerful than the Keck Observatory; its siting has drawn Native Hawaiian protests.

morrnah-simeona.name: Morrnah Simeona
morrnah-simeona.summary: Hawaiian healer, or kahuna lapaʻau (1913–1992), who taught her updated version of hoʻoponopono across the United States, Asia and Europe.

aku-aku.name: Aku-Aku
aku-aku.summary: A 1957 book by explorer Thor Heyerdahl about a Norwegian expedition's investigation of Easter Island and other Polynesian sites, which helped make the island's moai statues world-famous.

moai.name: Moai
moai.summary: Monolithic stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui people on Easter Island between 1250 and 1500, representing deified ancestors and set on platforms called ahu.

ki-i.name: Kiʻi
ki-i.summary: A religious image from Hawaiʻi believed able to hold the presence of a summoned god; also the name of the first man in Hawaiian religion.

woodrow-wilson.name: Woodrow Wilson
woodrow-wilson.summary: The 28th president of the United States, serving 1913 to 1921, the only Democrat to hold the office during the Progressive Era, who led the country through World War I and championed the League of Nations.

traditional-hawaiian-games.name: Pāʻani
traditional-hawaiian-games.summary: A general term for traditional Hawaiian play, games and chants, most centered on language, except the swinging game lele koali, played with a koali vine or a koali hao (metal chain).

2013-fifa-beach-soccer-world-cup.name: 2013 FIFA Beach Soccer World Cup
2013-fifa-beach-soccer-world-cup.summary: Beach soccer world championship held in Papeete, Tahiti, in September 2013, won by Russia over Spain in the final.
